topics.title: Khitab Hilaalul Washil
topics.istilah: Class notes spelling: Khitab Hilalul Wasil
topics.basis: Based on the Al Fathun Nawa framework · Volume 9 (Malay edition)

lead.tagline: Understanding an ayat through the links between words and ayat
paras: Khitab Hilalul Wasil is a method of explaining the Al Quran by linking ayat to ayat and word to word, where one explains the meaning of the other. In the Al Fathun Nawa framework, this link is called bacuhan pentafshilan (blending the detailed explanation). Its aim is to make the meaning clearer, deepen understanding and build a conviction that can be put into practice.

The author, Dr. Halo-N, uses several spellings, including Khitab Hilaalul Washil. This explanation uses Khitab Hilalul Wasil for the same method. In this discussion, the word khitab refers to the word or the chain of statements in the ayat being explained. To blend (membacuh) means to mix the explanation of meaning by showing links that the text supports.
refs: Reference: Al Fathun Nawa Volume 9, book p. 175–176 [PDF 264–265].

key.q: Which other ayat or word helps explain this meaning?
pills: A word made clear through an ayat
key.text: Bacuhan pentafshilan: blending the explanation by showing well-founded links of meaning.

items.name: Kaukaba Bil Munir
items.desc: Link the same or related words across ayat.

paras: Kaukaba Bil Munir looks for the explanation of one ayat or word through another ayat or word. In the working method described, the search pays attention to words that are the same or related in wording in different ayat. The explaining ayat is used to widen the understanding of the focus word.

The author links the word Wayatafakkaruuna in Ali Imran 3:191 with Yatafakkaruu in Ar Rum 30:8. The reader examines what is being thought about in both contexts, then explains how the second ayat helps in understanding the direction of thought in the first. Both ayat must be read in full so the link can be explained accurately.

To use it, choose the focus word, find an ayat with related wording, check the context and explain what the explaining ayat contributes. The conclusion must state the meaning gained from that link. The memory phrase is: find the wording and link the meaning.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 176–183 [PDF 265–272].

items.name: Thamarun Bil Munir
items.desc: Identify at least 3 essential traits and the defining ayat.

paras: Thamarun Bil Munir focuses on the definition of a word. The reader looks for ayat that explain the traits of the term so its meaning can be explained clearly. Repeating the original word without explaining its traits does not yet meet the aim of this method.

Volume 9 asks the reader to set out at least three essential traits stated by the ayat, then find the defining ayat that explain those traits. The author also links this step with Khamsul Gharib in Ta'wiilul Ma'ani. The three traits must come with supporting ayat, and their link to the term being studied must be explained.

The term patience (sabar) is the author's example, through Ali Imran 3:200, with an explanation that also links Al Baqarah 2:45. The author gives patience a specific meaning, including handing over to God what people are unable to do. That meaning must be presented as the author's own detailed summary, together with the reasons from the ayat used.
In your answer, state the term, set out its traits, explain the ayat that support each trait and build a definition from that explanation. The memory phrase is: term, traits and definition.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 185–194 [PDF 274–283]; the three-trait procedure on p. 188–189 [PDF 277–278].

items.name: Tafshiilul 'Aqid
items.desc: Identify mulk, maudha' and khitab; follow the statements in order.

paras: Tafshiilul 'Aqid develops the meaning of an ayat through the links between the words within the same ayat. A word or chain of khitab is explained by the khitab that follows it. The reader follows the order of the statements until the link between the parts of the ayat is understood.

The author uses the terms mulk, maudha' and khitab in this procedure. Maudha' is the topic of discussion. Mulk is the component whose position and direction must be identified according to the author's analysis. After identifying these components, the reader explains how the khitab that follow one another make the topic and the meaning of the ayat clear.

Hud 11:15 is the main example. The reader examines the link between the desire for the life of this world, its splendors, the full reward of deeds in this world and the statement that they will not be shortchanged there. The explanation is built by showing how each following part completes what is being told.

The working method is to read the full ayat, set out the topic and the components being explained, follow the khitab in order and summarise the whole message. The memory phrase is: explanation within the ayat.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 195–206 [PDF 284–295].

items.name: Bayaanul Ma'ani
items.desc: Use an explaining ayat to set out the effect of an action.

paras: Bayaanul Ma'ani looks for an ayat or chain of ayat that explains the direction of meaning of a statement. The author pays attention to the consequence that arises from an action in the first ayat and is explained further through the second ayat. The explanation may involve a good example or a warning limit.

The author's example links Az Zukhruf 43:36 with Al Baqarah 2:268. The first ayat touches on turning away from the reminder and the bond with Satan, while the second mentions Satan's push toward poverty and shameful deeds, and God's promise. This link is used to explain the attitude, its influence and its consequence.

The reader must identify the action being discussed, find the explaining ayat and show the link the context supports. If presenting a change from negative to positive, explain the corrective action and its support from the ayat. The memory phrase is: action and consequence.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 206–210 [PDF 295–299].

items.name: Faqqihil Muraad
items.desc: Examine different words that look alike in translation.

paras: Faqqihil Muraad develops the explanation by examining two terms that may look the same in a short translation. The reader looks for the differences in meaning, position or classification that the context of the ayat explains. This method trains us to notice how precisely terms are used.

The author compares Raji'uun in Al Baqarah 2:156 with Tuhsyaruun in Ali Imran 3:158. He raises the question of both being explained with the word 'return'. In a presentation, the reader must examine the difference in wording and context, including the meaning of being gathered in Tuhsyaruun. Do not assume that a similar short translation has settled the meaning of both terms.

The working method is to choose the pair of terms, read each ayat, set out the similarity that causes confusion and explain the difference with evidence. The conclusion states why that difference matters for understanding the ayat. The memory phrase is: tell the meanings of terms apart.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 214–217 [PDF 303–306].

items.name: Tafshiilul Jalil
items.desc: Follow the links between khitab to the whole message of the ayat.

paras: Tafshiilul Jalil explains an ayat through the continuing meaning between khitab. The topic is explained by the first khitab, then the explanation carries on through the following khitab to the end of the ayat. The aim is to understand clearly what the whole ayat is telling.

Hud 11:15 and Al Baqarah 2:26 are the author's examples. In Al Baqarah 2:26, the reader follows the statements about the parable, the attitude of believers and of those who reject, the questioning of the parable and the statement about guidance and going astray. The conclusion of the ayat is also noted so the explanation does not stop before the statement is complete.

This method overlaps with Tafshiilul 'Aqid in following khitab in order within one ayat. For practice, we can focus Tafshiilul Jalil on explaining the chain up to the whole message. This focus helps the presentation, without claiming that 'Aqid is limited to a single link. The memory phrase is: a chain of explanation up to the conclusion.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 222–226 [PDF 311–315].

items.name: Ruhul Idhafa'
items.desc: Examine how a statement is attributed to God and to people in the author's framework.

paras: Ruhul Idhafa' pays attention to words that involve the position of God and of people. The reader examines who is referred to, the direction of the relationship and the meaning of the action in that context. The author uses the classification of qadim (eternal) and majazi (figurative) to explain the difference in status within his framework.

The examples are Nasta'iin in Al Fatihah 1:5 and Tanshuruu in Muhammad 47:7. The first ayat holds a request for help from God. The second holds a call to help Allah and a statement of His help to people. The explanation must show the different directions of the relationship and how the author explains human responsibility through it.

In his specific explanation, the author links helping God with human work that develops life. He also uses the phrase 'God's inability' in the context of this philosophy of work. That phrase is the author's own interpretation on p. 228, not the wording of the ayat; a presenter must keep the attribution and explain its context.
The working method is to identify the parties referred to, compare the contexts and explain the difference in status according to the source. The memory phrase is: parties, relationship and status.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 226–231 [PDF 315–320].

items.name: Hilalul Khusuf
items.desc: Go deeper into a word whose meaning is still hidden.

paras: Hilalul Khusuf develops the explanation when the meaning of an ayat is still unclear or hidden. The author likens it to an eclipsed moon. The reader examines the word in depth until the difference in meaning can be explained clearly.

At Taubah 9:103 is the example, through Tutahhiruhum and Watuzakkiihim bihaa. The short translations 'cleanse' and 'purify' can look almost the same. This method asks the reader to investigate the link and the difference between the two meanings in the context of the charity the ayat mentions.

For practice, state what is still unclear, set out the words to compare and present evidence from the ayat for the explanation. Do not build a difference from assumption alone. The conclusion must explain how the analysis helps in understanding the whole statement. The memory phrase is: the unclear made clear.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 242–244 [PDF 331–333].

Similar wording is the starting point; the link in meaning must be explained.

notes.heading: Accuracy Notes
items: The introduction names 7; the full explanation also adds Hilalul Khusuf as the 8th method.
Terms and examples follow the author's usage.

sections.heading: Basic meaning and aim of the method
paras: Put simply, this method invites the reader to ask which other ayat or word helps explain what is being read. Sometimes the explanation is in the same ayat. Sometimes we need to examine another ayat that uses related wording, defines a term or explains the consequence of an action.

The aim is to avoid reading that stops at a short translation without understanding how statements connect. When two ayat are linked, the reader must explain the point that links them. Similar words can be where the search starts, but the reasoning of the explanation needs attention to the context of the whole ayat.

In Volume 9, the author pictures this explanation through the link between moonlight and sunlight. That picture is a metaphor for meaning made clear through an explaining ayat. To use the method, we must still identify the word, the ayat and their link in meaning explicitly.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 175–178 [PDF 264–267].

sections.heading: The eight methods of bacuhan pentafshilan
paras: The eight methods explained are Kaukaba Bil Munir, Thamarun Bil Munir, Tafshiilul 'Aqid, Bayaanul Ma'ani, Faqqihil Muraad, Tafshiilul Jalil, Ruhul Idhafa' and Hilalul Khusuf. Each method gives a particular focus to the link that is to be made clear.

The introduction on page 176 names seven stages, then the discussion on page 242 adds an eighth method, Hilalul Khusuf. So this explanation covers all eight methods, as in the author's full explanation. The spelling Khusuf follows Volume 9; the exam notes write Khusus in that part.

The differences between the methods help in choosing how to explain an ayat. However, some methods overlap. Tafshiilul 'Aqid and Tafshiilul Jalil, for example, both explain the chain of khitab within one ayat. We need to make the focus of the presentation clear without building an absolute separation the source does not state.

sections.heading: How to set out an explanation and an exam answer
paras: Set out the answer through the definition, the aim, how to use the method, an example ayat and the conclusion. Start by stating the link to be studied. Then present the focus ayat and the explaining ayat, or the chain of khitab in the same ayat. Explain what each part contributes to understanding.

For Kaukaba Bil Munir, state the wording that links the ayat. For Thamarun Bil Munir, set out the traits that build the definition. For Bayaanul Ma'ani, explain the action and its consequence. The choice of method must come with a reason so the answer shows the way of analysis, not just the name of the method.

The conclusion answers what has become clearer after the explanation. Tell apart the wording of the ayat, the translation, the author's summary and your own example of applying it. This makes the explanation more precise and easier to check.

sections.heading: Example of a full explanation
paras: Kaukaba Bil Munir is a method of explaining the meaning of a word or ayat through another ayat that helps explain it. The author links the word for thinking in Ali Imran 3:191 with the related word in Ar Rum 30:8. Similar wording is the starting point for examining the link in meaning between the two ayat.

In Ali Imran 3:191, the reader notes the link between remembering God, thinking about the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the acknowledgement that this creation has a purpose. Ar Rum 30:8 helps the reading by directing attention to thought and to creation based on truth and an appointed term. That link must be explained by reading the context of each ayat.

So the meaning of thinking is widened through what is thought about and the statements that come with it. The reader understands that naming the act alone does not yet explain the direction of thought. This is the result of practising Kaukaba Bil Munir: making the focus word clear through an ayat linked in meaning.

sections.heading: Summary to understand and remember
paras: The eight focus words are wording, definition, explanation within the ayat, consequence, difference of terms, chain of explanation, status and the unclear. Match each word with the name of the method and one example ayat. This order is a memory aid for learning.

When reading, ask what needs to be made clear, where the explaining ayat or khitab is, and what the evidence for that link is. Then state the meaning that results. In this way, bacuhan pentafshilan becomes an explaining process the reader can follow and assess.

topics.title: Syariat Khafiah
topics.basis: Based on the Al Fathun Nawa framework · Volumes 6 and 9 (Malay edition)

lead.tagline: Understanding the guidance of an ayat and shaping how we live
paras: Syariah Khofiah invites us to read the Al Quran by examining what God tells, commands and calls for, then understanding how that guidance shapes conviction and action. In the Al Fathun Nawa framework, this reading aims to produce people who take heed, grow mature and work for progress in life.

The term the author, Dr. Halo-N, uses most is Syariat Khafiah. This explanation uses the name Syariah Khofiah, as in the study notes, for the same concept in his work. Volume 9 introduces it as the 15th method of detailed explanation (pentafshilan), which classifies the position of an ayat into ten levels. Those ten levels help us recognise the direction an ayat teaches in and describe how it is practised.
refs: Reference: Al Fathun Nawa Volume 9, book p. 356–358 [PDF 445–447]; Syariah Khofiah Exam Notes, table of ten levels.

key.q: What does this ayat teach me to understand and do?
key.text: Classifying the direction an ayat teaches in, and applying it as conviction and as practice in life.

items.name: Rabbi Amri
items.desc: Notice the creation and ordering of nature.

paras: Rabbi Amri focuses on the work of God that the ayat tells of, including the creation and ordering of nature. We read that statement to recognise God's power, place our hope in Him and take heed from the creation we observe.

The study notes cite Ibrahim 14:19 as the basis and As Sajdah 32:4 as the example. Both direct attention to the creation of the heavens and the earth. In the explanation, we can show that nature becomes something to observe that reminds people of their Creator. Observing creation pushes people to study and value the order of nature.

The fitting practice is to read, observe and study creation with awareness of God. That knowledge builds a sense of responsibility toward nature and one's own work. The memory phrase for this level is: God's work.

items.name: Khitaabul 'Ajil
items.desc: Understand the command and answer the guidance earnestly.

paras: Khitaabul 'Ajil pays attention to God's commands that must be answered and made a conviction for life. The reader identifies what is commanded, understands its meaning and carries it out earnestly. The idea of hastening stresses the attitude of answering the guidance, with the action suited to the context of the command.

Al Anfal 8:24 is used as the basis for answering a call that gives life. Ali Imran 3:200 is the example, holding a call to be patient, to strengthen each other's patience, to stay ready and to have taqwa. The reader must explain the link between that command and the success the ayat aims at.

As a practice exercise, someone facing a hard responsibility can organise the tasks, keep discipline and work together. This example is an application for learning; it must be kept apart from the original wording of the ayat. The memory phrase is: God's command.

items.name: Baalighatul Aayah
items.desc: Build discipline and readiness to carry responsibility.

paras: Baalighatul Aayah invites people to grow mature through the teaching of the ayat. Maturity shows in the ability to understand responsibility, control oneself and take well-founded action. The reader examines which traits are being shaped and how they can be applied.

The notes use Al Muddaththir 74:1–7 as the example. This chain of ayat holds the instructions to rise and warn, magnify God, purify one's clothes, keep away from filth, mind one's attitude in giving and be patient for God's sake. In the frame of this level, those instructions are explained as training that shapes a self ready to carry responsibility.

The practice is to train discipline, keep clean and carry duties with patience and awareness of God. When answering an exam, state the trait of maturity the ayat supports and explain the behaviour that shows it. The memory phrase is: maturity of the self.

items.name: Nidaa ul Kubraa
items.desc: Understand what is asked for and link prayer with effort.

paras: Nidaa ul Kubra focuses on the prayers of the prophets recorded in the Al Quran. The reader understands what is asked for, why it matters and the attitude the request shapes. A prayer that is understood gives direction to a person's effort.

An Naml 27:19 is the example of Prophet Sulaiman's prayer, asking to be moved to give thanks for favours, do righteous deeds that please God and be admitted among the righteous servants through God's mercy. The explanation must link gratitude with deeds and with being among the righteous.

The practice is to pray with understanding, recognise one's favours and work at good deeds. Someone who asks to be grateful also strives to use favours responsibly. The memory phrase is: a prayer that is understood.

items.name: Fathul 'Arif
items.desc: Know God through the statements of revelation.

paras: Fathul 'Arif explains how God introduces Himself to people through revelation. The reader recognises the statements about God that the ayat conveys and understands what the bond between people and God asks of them.

Taha 20:14 is a clear example. The ayat introduces Allah, states His oneness and holds the command to worship and establish solat to remember Him. Knowing God is directly linked to the direction of worship and to people's remembrance of Him.

Rabbi Amri highlights God's work, while Fathul 'Arif highlights knowing God through revelation. Both can meet in one ayat. In a presentation, make clear which angle is being explained so the reason for choosing the level is understood. The memory phrase is: knowing God.

items.name: Rafi'ul Hayat
items.desc: Raise the quality of life through knowledge, effort and deeds.

paras: Rafi'ul Hayat explains guidance that helps people raise the quality and rank of their lives. The reader understands the link between effort, deeds and their results. Progress demands earnest action and responsibility for the quality of one's work.

The notes cite Al An'am 6:83 and 6:132 and An Najm 53:39–40. An Najm links a person to his effort and states that his effort will be shown. In the explanation, this link pushes the reader to increase knowledge, skill and diligence.

As an example of applying it, a student draws up a revision timetable, assesses weak spots and improves the way of studying. Progress is explained through effort that can be identified, without turning the ayat into a guarantee that every personal wish will be met. The memory phrase is: raising life.

items.name: Amthaalul Hilal
items.desc: Study resources and bring out their benefit responsibly.

paras: Amthaalul Hilal pays attention to resources and signs that must be studied until their benefit shows in life. In the notes, that resource is linked with the furqan of progress. The reader learns to see creation as material for exploring knowledge and benefit for people.

The notes cite Al An'am 6:104, Yunus 10:101 and Al Hadid 57:25. Al Hadid mentions iron with its strength and its benefits for people, in the context of the book, the balance and justice. The explanation can show how a resource needs knowledge and responsible use to produce benefit.

Studying materials, building tools and improving technology are examples of application that can be discussed. Such an example is an explanation of practice, not a claim that the ayat names any particular modern technology. The memory phrase is: resources become benefit.

items.name: Nurul 'Ibrah
items.desc: Take examples and limits from the stories.

paras: Nurul Ibrah invites the reader to take lessons from the stories recorded in the Al Quran. We examine attitudes, actions and consequences in a story to recognise the examples to follow and the mistakes to avoid.

Yusuf 12:3 and 12:111 are important references in the notes. Yusuf 12:111 stresses that there are lessons in the stories for people of understanding. When explaining a story, the reader must tie the lesson to what the ayat actually states.

The practice is to review one's own decisions against the lessons learned. For example, a story that shows the result of envy helps the reader weigh the effect of that attitude on human relationships. Avoid adding events or dialogue that are not in the text. The memory phrase is: the story becomes a lesson.

items.name: Hujjatul Ihsaan
items.desc: Arrange the evidence and present the explanation well.

paras: Hujjatul Ihsan focuses on well-founded argument and on conveying the truth in a good way. The reader understands the content of the argument, the evidence that supports it and how to explain the link between the evidence and the conclusion.

The notes cite An Nahl 16:125, which holds the call with wisdom, good advice and debate in the best way. Al An'am 6:149 mentions the conclusive argument that belongs to Allah. Taha 20:27–28 reminds us of the importance of speech that can be understood.

The practice is to set out the issue, present relevant evidence and give clear reasons. We listen to objections and answer the points raised accurately. The memory phrase is: argue with evidence and in a good way.

items.name: Bayaanul 'Aqid
items.desc: Understand the principles and align actions with the guidance.

paras: Bayaanul 'Aqid pays attention to the statements that form the core of conviction in religion and in belief in God. The reader examines the principle the ayat states and how that principle guides life. Conviction needs an understanding of its basis and earnestness in showing it in practice.

The notes link this level with Ar Rum 30:30, Ali Imran 3:7, Al Maidah 5:48 and Al Jathiyah 45:18. In the explanation, the reader explains the link between fitrah, the place of the ayat that form the basis of the Book and the need to follow guidance. The explanation must follow the context of each ayat and explain the links made.

The practice is to check whether a principle one holds has support from the ayat, then assess whether one's actions are in line with it. We must tell apart the statement of the ayat from the detailed summary built from it. The memory phrase is: the core of conviction.
refs: Reference for the ten levels: Syariah Khofiah Exam Notes, pages 1–7; the classification is confirmed in Volume 9, book p. 357–358 [PDF 446–447]. The practice explanations above include examples of application for learning.

sections.heading: Basic meaning of Syariah Khofiah
paras: Put simply, Syariah Khofiah is an approach to explaining an ayat in order to understand the teaching for life held in God's reports, commands and calls. The reader examines the meaning of the ayat, the importance of its guidance and the change that must show in life. The main question is: what does this ayat teach me to understand and do?

For example, when an ayat calls people to be patient, the reader must understand the kind of patience meant and the situations that need it. That understanding turns into perseverance, self-control and earnestness in carrying out responsibilities. The explanation of practice must connect to the statement of the ayat, not be built from assumptions cut off from the text.

In Volume 6, the author explains Syariat Hukamat and Syariat Khafiah as two angles of teaching that must be practised together. Hukamat pays attention to rulings and rules, while Khafiah explains the teaching that matures life. In his framework, the two complete each other. Syariah Khofiah gives no reason to set aside responsibilities the ayat states.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 712–714 [PDF 781–783]; Volume 9, book p. 606–609 [PDF 695–698].

sections.heading: Learning aims
paras: The aim is to form readers who understand the importance of an ayat and take heed from it. The author uses the term Muzakkirin for people who receive and practise the reminder, and Mu'riduun for people who turn away from or ignore the guidance. In study, these terms invite us to check our own attitude toward the ayat we read.

The progress described covers maturity of thought, mastery of knowledge, quality of work and humanity. We need to ask whether reading the ayat has helped us become more trustworthy, earnest, fair and useful to others. That way, understanding has an effect that can be described in life.

The author also stresses the enlightening of life, the building of a positive attitude and taking examples from the stories. All of this needs careful reading. Memorising the names of the levels helps memory, but understanding the proofs and the forms of practice is what lets us use the method.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 713 [PDF 782]; Volume 9, book p. 607–610 [PDF 696–699].

sections.heading: How to set out an explanation and an exam answer
paras: Volume 9 asks for an explanation that covers the proof, the definition, the importance and the form of practice, with an example ayat for each level. This order helps the answer be complete. Start with the name of the level and its meaning, present the relevant ayat, then explain why that ayat fits the level.

Then explain the importance of the ayat's teaching and give a concrete example of practice. For example, for Nidaa ul Kubra, explain the meaning of the prayer in An Naml 27:19, the link between gratitude and righteous deeds, and the effort to use favours responsibly. The conclusion must sum up the change asked of the reader.

Volume 6 also sets out a reading procedure through the revealing ayat, the method of interpretation, the reminder, the statement and the resolution. The resolution is a summary that explains the direction of action once the ayat is understood. It must come out of the explanation before it, so the answer does not end with general advice unrelated to the ayat.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 609–610 [PDF 698–699]; Volume 6, Introduction p. lx–lxiv [PDF 61–65].

sections.heading: Example of a full explanation
paras: Nidaa ul Kubra is the level of Syariah Khofiah that invites people to understand the prayers of the prophets recorded in the Al Quran. In An Naml 27:19, Prophet Sulaiman asks to be moved to give thanks for God's favours, do righteous deeds that please Him and be among the righteous servants through His mercy. This prayer shows the link between awareness of favours and the effort to do good.

Its importance is that the reader understands the direction of his request to God. Gratitude demands awareness of favours and using them responsibly. When someone prays to do righteous deeds, he must also examine his actions so they bring good. An example of practice is using knowledge to help others and using time to fulfil responsibilities.

So learning Nidaa ul Kubra forms people who pray with understanding and link prayer with effort. This is the resolution of that explanation: making an understood request the direction for shaping attitude and action.

sections.heading: Summary to understand and remember
paras: The ten focus words are work, command, maturity, prayer, knowing, raising, resources, lessons, argument and conviction. Match each word with its level name, one example ayat and one form of practice. This list of words is a memory aid for the notes, not the original wording of the Al Quran.

To understand any ayat, ask four things: what the ayat states, what direction it teaches in, why that teaching matters and how it is practised. Check the answer against the whole context of the ayat and related ayat. In this way, learning Syariah Khofiah helps us move from recognising guidance to showing practice that can be explained clearly.

topics.title: Ta'wiilul Ma'ani
topics.basis: Based on the Al Fathun Nawa framework · Volumes 6 and 9 (Malay edition)

lead.tagline: Understanding what an ayat wants to tell
paras: Ta'wilul Ma'ani is a method of explanation for understanding what an ayat wants to tell. In the Al Fathun Nawa framework, the reader examines the order of the statements, identifies the topic and follows the explanation that clarifies that topic. The aim is to gain an understanding that is deep, easy to remember and able to shape a conviction for life.

The author, Dr. Halo-N, uses the spellings Ta'wiilul Ma'ani and Ta'awiilul Ma'ani. This explanation refers to his method as set out in Volume 6 and developed in Volume 9. Its focus is the link between the governing word (kalimah takluk), the topic of discussion, the explaining content and the summary of meaning.
refs: Reference: Al Fathun Nawa Volume 6, book p. 632–634 [PDF 701–703]; Volume 9, book p. 300–302 [PDF 389–391].

key.q: What does this ayat want to tell?
key.text: Understanding the purpose of an ayat through the link between its topic and the statements that explain it.

paras: Mulk is the term for what governs the topic, which the author explains as the power of direction and the aim of the topic. In the working method, the governing word helps identify the direction and pattern of the statement being analysed. Examples of governing words are La'allahum, Laqad, Ulaaika and Qad, depending on the method and its context.

Maudha' is the topic or main purpose of the discussion. The reader decides what the statement focuses on, then links the explaining content to that topic. The topic must be identified from the text, not set simply because it suits the issue one wants to discuss.

Khitab is the directional content the words carry for the topic. It may be a word or a chain of ayat that explains the topic, depending on the method. In short, mulk helps set the governing direction, maudha' sets the topic and khitab makes the content clear.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 865 [PDF 954]; Volume 6, book p. 639–642 [PDF 708–711].

items.name: Dhomir Taqaddim
items.tag: One ayat · Topic at the end
items.desc: Explanation → Topic

paras: Dhomir Taqaddim understands an ayat guided by the topic at the end of the ayat. The khitab before it explains the meaning and direction of that topic. The reader follows the content from the start of the ayat and links it to the result stated at its end.

The author lists markers such as La'allakum, La'allahum and Inkuntum to recognise the pattern of the method. These markers must be checked against the whole ayat. The presence of a word is the starting point of the analysis; the link between the topic and the khitab decides the explanation built.

Al Baqarah 2:186 is the original example. The author draws attention to La'allahum yarshuduun at the end of the ayat. The reader links the aim of being guided with the statements about God's closeness, asking in prayer, answering His call and believing in Him. The memory phrase is: one ayat, topic at the end.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 639–643 [PDF 708–712]; the example starts on p. 643 [PDF 712].

items.name: Dhomir Ta'akhkhir
items.tag: One ayat · Topic at the start
items.desc: Topic → Explanation

paras: Dhomir Ta'akhkhir understands an ayat guided by the topic at the start of the ayat, then follows the khitab after it to the end of the ayat. The author sums up this pattern as the topic or consequence at the start, and the explanation after it.

Among the governing words listed are Inna, Inni, Qul, Qad and Laqad. The reader must decide what is introduced after the governing word and how the rest of the statement explains it. This link helps us follow the content of the ayat in order.

Yusuf 12:111 is the original example, with the word Laqad and the statement about lessons in the stories for people of understanding. The rest of the ayat explains the place of those stories and mentions confirmation, explanation, guidance and mercy. The reader links that explanation to the topic of lessons being discussed. The memory phrase is: one ayat, topic at the start.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 654–658 [PDF 723–727]; example on p. 658–659 [PDF 727–728].

items.name: Dhomir Taqaddimul Awwal
items.tag: Chain of ayat · Conclusion at the end
items.desc: Explaining ayat → Concluding ayat

paras: Dhomir Taqaddimul Awwal reads a chain of ayat by paying attention to the topic or result in the last ayat, which the earlier ayat explain. The reader examines who or what that conclusion refers to, then goes back to the earlier explanation.

The author lists governing words such as Ulaaika, Ulaaikallazii, Ulaaika lahum and Watilka. In this method, the explanation lies in several earlier ayat, while the result lies in a later ayat. The main difference from Taqaddim is that the analysis covers a chain of ayat.

Al Baqarah 2:5 is the original example. The statement that they are upon guidance from their God and are the successful ones is linked to the traits explained in the ayat before it, especially 2:2–4. So the reader explains who is meant through the earlier explanation. The memory phrase is: many ayat, conclusion at the end.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 670–675 [PDF 739–744].

items.name: Dhomir Taqaddimul Aakhir
items.tag: Chain of ayat · Topic at the front
items.desc: Topic ayat → Explaining ayat

paras: Dhomir Taqaddimul Aakhir reads a chain of ayat where the topic or result is introduced in the first ayat, then made clear by the ayat that follow. The reader follows the explaining chain to understand the statement introduced at the beginning.

Al Mukminun 23:1 is the original example: the statement about the success of the believers. The following ayat, 23:2–11, explain the traits, conduct and results linked to them. The explanation must show the link between the statement of success and the details that follow.

The steps are to set out the topic ayat, identify the explaining ayat and explain how each one links to the topic. The conclusion sums up the picture formed by the whole chain. The memory phrase is: many ayat, topic at the front.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 683–689 [PDF 752–758].

items.name: Dhomir Kulli Awla
items.tag: Direct meaning of the whole ayat
items.desc: Understand the statement as a whole.

paras: Dhomir Kulli Awla understands the direct, single-layer meaning of an ayat without rearranging it. According to the author, this method is used when the meaning of the ayat is easy to grasp and does not follow the patterns of the other basic methods.

The explanation lies in the words that make up the ayat, while the topic and its importance are understood through the whole meaning. The author names short ayat and oath ayat as among the forms often found with this method. In Volume 9, Bismillahir rahmanir rahim is given as an example.

The reader explains the meaning of the words in order, links them to the whole statement and sums up the purpose of the ayat. Related ayat can be used to strengthen the explanation. The direct meaning still needs care with language and context. The memory phrase is: the direct meaning of the whole ayat.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 701–705 [PDF 770–774]; Volume 9, book p. 865–866 [PDF 954–955].

groups.heading: 3 Additional Levels

items.name: Khamsul Gharib
items.desc: Ask the same question 5 times; give 5 well-founded angles of answer.

paras: Khamsul Gharib deepens understanding by asking the same question five times and giving five different answers. The author's question is: what does this ayat want to tell? Each answer brings out a different angle of teaching, with support that can be explained.

This method helps the reader develop the content of an argument and trains fluency in explaining. Five answers do not mean changing the meaning at will. The reader must explain how each answer links to the ayat, tell apart overlapping content and check the explanation against related ayat.

The author uses the end of Yusuf 12:76, about the raising of ranks and there being one more knowing above every owner of knowledge. His five angles cover the importance of rank, the need to increase knowledge, acknowledging those with more knowledge, using knowledge for progress and the problem of looking down on knowledge.

All of this develops the teaching within the author's framework. When presenting the quote from the end of the ayat, say it is part of Yusuf 12:76 and check the context of the whole ayat too. The memory phrase is: one question, five angles of answer.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 598–601 [PDF 687–690].

items.name: Ra'sil 'Ulum
items.desc: Explain the words of a leader or a figure of learning.

paras: Dhamir Ra'sil 'Ulum extends the use of Ta'wilul Ma'ani to the words of leaders and sages that can be a subject of reflection or an example. The reader examines what is said, the context of the statement, the explaining content and the lesson that can be drawn.

As practice, a statement on the importance of knowledge can be explained by identifying the topic of knowledge, the reasons given and the action suggested. This practice builds the skill of commenting and giving a well-founded view. It applies the method to a human text.

A leader's words must be judged on their content and the evidence that supports them. Being used as practice material does not make them an ayat of the Al Quran or a proof equal to it. The memory phrase is: explaining a leader's words.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 301–302 [PDF 390–391] and 867–869 [PDF 956–958].

items.name: Ra'sis Syahid
items.desc: Explain the message of a poem, pantun, gurindam or lyric.

paras: Dhamir Ra'sis Syahid extends the method to poems, pantun, gurindam, syair, song lyrics and similar works. The reader examines the observation, imagery and message the work carries, then explains the lesson worth considering.

In practice, set out the theme of the work, explain the role of a stanza or phrase and show how that part builds the whole message. Pay attention to the context and the figurative language so the conclusion does not drift away from the work.

The lesson of a work is the result of analysing a human text. It must be weighed and kept apart from the statements of revelation. The aim of the practice is to build the ability to understand and comment carefully. The memory phrase is: explaining the message of a work.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 302 [PDF 391] and 867–869 [PDF 956–958].

groups.note: Ra'sil 'Ulum and Ra'sis Syahid extend the method to human texts; keep them apart from ayat of the Al Quran.

formula.heading: Memory Formula
chips: Extra: 5 answers · words of figures · works of poets

notes.heading: Notes
items: Terms and patterns follow the author's usage. One word alone is not enough; check the order and context of the ayat.

sections.heading: Basic meaning of Ta'wilul Ma'ani
paras: Put simply, Ta'wilul Ma'ani helps us answer the question: what does this ayat want to convey? We read the full ayat, understand its language and set out the link between the topic and the statements that explain it. The explanation must show how the conclusion comes out of the order of the ayat.

The author bases this method on Mantiq Tajwid Al Ahaadith. In his explanation, Mantiq Al Ahaadith refers to how statements are worked through, while Tajwid Al Ahaadith refers to the arrangement of the statements of the Al Quran. These terms explain how to examine and work through the links of meaning in the text.

For example, an ayat may hold a command at its start and an aim at its end. The reader needs to know the link between that command and that aim. In a chain of ayat, the topic may appear first and then be explained by several following ayat, or the conclusion may appear after the explanation.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 632–633 [PDF 701–702].

sections.heading: Aim and importance of learning it
paras: The aim is to bring out the ideas, concepts, principles, philosophy, teaching and wisdom that can be understood through the ayat. The author also stresses the sweetness of understanding: the sense of being drawn in when the reader can clearly follow what the ayat tells.

In study, this understanding helps us explain an ayat in an orderly way. We know what its topic is, where its explanation lies and what summary the whole statement supports. So the explanation has a direction the listener can follow.

Volume 9 sums up its importance as the effort to know what each ayat we read and discuss wants to tell. So learning must involve practice in explaining ayat, not just memorising the names of the methods.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 633–635 [PDF 702–704]; Volume 9, book p. 302 [PDF 391].

sections.heading: Five basic methods and three additions
paras: Volume 6 introduces five basic methods: Dhomir Taqaddim, Dhomir Ta'akhkhir, Dhomir Taqaddimul Awwal, Dhomir Taqaddimul Aakhir and Dhomir Kulli Awla. The first four pay attention to where the topic and its explanation sit in one ayat or a chain of ayat. Kulli Awla examines the direct meaning that can be understood from the whole statement.

Volume 9 adds Dhamir Khamsul Gharib, Dhamir Ra'sil 'Ulum and Dhamir Ra'sis Syahid. Khamsul Gharib deepens the explanation through a repeated question. The last two extend the method to the words of leaders or sages and to works such as poems and gurindam.

The five basic methods help read the order of an ayat. The three additions build practice in explaining and widen where the method is used. The explanation must keep the difference between the ayat of the Al Quran and the human texts analysed with the method.
refs: Reference: Volume 6, book p. 633 [PDF 702]; Volume 9, book p. 301–302 [PDF 390–391].

sections.heading: Six basic steps
paras: First, choose an ayat or chain of ayat and set out the governing word and the pattern of the method. Second, identify the maudha' or topic in focus. Third, read the whole text again and set out the khitab that explains the topic.

Fourth, explain the meaning of each khitab from its language and link it directly to the topic. Fifth, use other directly related ayat to strengthen the explanation. The author calls these supporting ayat Verse Lord's Authority. Sixth, sum up the purpose, aim and meaning that can shape a conviction for life.

These steps must be used according to the pattern of the method chosen. Some patterns happen within one ayat, while others involve several ayat. Do not fix the span of the reading before the topic and its explanation are identified.

sections.heading: Example of a full explanation and exam guide
paras: Dhomir Taqaddimul Awwal is a method of understanding the conclusion of a chain of ayat through the explanation that comes before it. In Al Baqarah 2:5, the statement about guidance and success must be linked to the traits of the group explained in the ayat before it. Ayat 2:2–4 give the explanation that helps identify that group.

The reader explains the link between the guidance, faith, deeds and certainty mentioned in that chain of ayat. Then he shows how the statement 'those are the successful' links to the earlier explanation. So the word 'those' has a clear reference in the explanation.

In conclusion, this method helps us understand success through the traits the ayat explain, by following the order of the statements up to the final summary. In an exam answer, present the definition of the method, where the topic sits, the explaining khitab, the supporting ayat and the conclusion. Explain why you chose the method so the reader can follow the analysis.

sections.heading: Summary to understand and remember
paras: Remember the five basic patterns: one ayat with the topic at the end; one ayat with the topic at the start; several ayat with the conclusion at the end; several ayat with the topic at the front; and the direct meaning of the whole ayat. Match these patterns with the method names and their original examples.

Remember the three additions: Khamsul Gharib asks one question with five answers, Ra'sil 'Ulum explains the words of a leader or sage, and Ra'sis Syahid explains works such as poems and gurindam. This summary helps memory; real use still needs reading the text and clear reasons.

topics.title: Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul
topics.basis: Based on the Al Fathun Nawa framework · Volume 9 (Malay edition)

lead.tagline: Understanding the problem in an ayat and working toward its solution
paras: When we read the Al Quran, we need to understand what the ayat conveys and why it matters for life. In the Al Fathun Nawa framework, this second question is explained through the method of Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul. The method invites the reader to examine the implied chain of events, identify the dilemma, look for the way to solve it and take lessons from the result of that solution.

This explanation uses the terms of the author, Dr. Halo-N. In Volume 9, he introduces Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul as the thirteenth method of detailed explanation (pentafshilan). The term pentafshilan is used for an explanation that makes clear the meaning and sense of an ayat. The aim is an understanding that can shape conviction and action in life.
refs: Main reference: Volume 9, book p. 11–19 [PDF 100–108].

key.label: What does it mean?
key.text: Examining the problem an ayat points to, explaining its effects and finding a solution through the guidance of the Al Quran.

items.name: Chain of Events
items.desc: A series of situations or attitudes the ayat points to.

paras: The first element is the implied chain of events (rentetan peristiwa). It means a series of situations or attitudes that can be explained from the statement of the ayat. That series must be based on the words of the ayat and their links of meaning. The aim is to show the problem clearly, without adding names, dates or events that are not stated.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 12–19 and 28–29 [PDF 101–108 and 117–118].

items.name: Dilemma
items.desc: A problem or tangle that needs untangling.

paras: The second element is the dilemma. In the author's usage, a dilemma refers to a problem or tangle that needs a solution. A dilemma may relate to ignorance, refusing guidance, weak action or the harmful effect of an attitude. The main question is: what problem is being shown to people?
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 12–19 and 28–29 [PDF 101–108 and 117–118].

items.name: Philosophy of the Solution
items.desc: Principles and actions to put things right.

paras: The third element is the philosophy of the solution. Here, philosophy means a principle or direction of action explained from the guidance of the ayat in order to untangle the problem. If the problem is a refusal to examine, the solution must involve examining. If the problem is the loss that comes from neglecting time, the solution must involve using time in a way that builds life.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 12–19 and 28–29 [PDF 101–108 and 117–118].

items.name: Nostalgia
items.desc: The sweetness and benefit after the problem is solved.

paras: The fourth element is nostalgia. The author uses this term for the sweetness or good that results once the dilemma is solved. In this context, nostalgia refers to the experience of change, understanding and calm that can become a conviction for life. So the reader must explain what benefit comes from the solution, not just state that a problem is solved.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 12–19 and 28–29 [PDF 101–108 and 117–118].

steps.heading: 4 Basic Steps
items: Read the ayat and identify the words of the dilemma
Set out the problem it raises
Explain the implied chain of events
Explain the solution and its benefit

lists.heading: 7 Levels of an Exam Answer
items: Effects of the chain of dilemma
The path of the philosophy of the solution
Summary: include 3 supporting ayat and explain how they connect.
lists.note: "God's dilemma with people" is the author's term for the relationship between God's guidance and people's attitudes.

example.heading: Example · Muhammad 47:24
rows: Refusing to reflect deeply on the Al Quran (tadabbur).
Examine the ayat, understand it and take the lesson.
Clearer understanding and a more open attitude.
example.note: This example is a summary of the explanation, not a quotation of the ayat.

notes.heading: Notes
items: An implied explanation must rest on the ayat; do not treat it as historical proof of why the ayat was revealed.

sections.heading: Basic meaning of the concept
paras: Put simply, Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul is a method of explaining an ayat by examining the problem it points to behind its statement, then looking for a solution that brings good to life. Its focus is the link between the statement of the ayat, people's attitudes, the effects of those attitudes and the change that must be made.

Picture someone reading an ayat that calls people to think. The reader does not stop at the meaning of the word "think". He asks: what problem arises when people do not think? What is its effect on their decisions and actions? How does the call help them overcome the problem? What change can be felt after they act?

These questions show the direction of renewal (pengashlihan), that is, improvement worked for through understanding and carrying out the guidance. The reader moves from recognising the problem to improving attitudes and situations. The memory formula is: chain of events, dilemma, philosophy of the solution and nostalgia.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 12–19 [PDF 101–108]; the memory formula is a short order for explaining.

sections.heading: Its link to Asbaabun Nuzul
paras: In Volumes 1 and 2, the author explains Asbaabun Nuzul through the events, attitudes and behaviour of society in the time of Muhammad's messengership. Those events help explain the importance of the ayat and the lessons that can be taken from it.

In Volume 9, the author widens that approach. He invites the reader to examine the implied chain of events the ayat suggests, including problems of life that can recur in later times. So attention is given to why people need the guidance of the ayat and how that guidance can be used to solve problems.

Here we must tell apart two kinds of statement. A historical account of the events behind the revelation of an ayat needs historical proof. An explanation of an implied chain of events is the result of reading and explaining the ayat in detail. When presenting an implied explanation, we can say "this ayat points to a problem" or "in the author's framework, this ayat is explained as". We do not turn the picture we build into a claim that a particular historical event really happened.
refs: Reference: Volume 1, book p. 20–23 [PDF 129–132]; Volume 2, book p. 21–24 [PDF 82–85]; Volume 9, book p. 12–15 [PDF 101–104].

sections.heading: Understanding the terms God's dilemma and people's dilemma
paras: The author uses the phrases "God's dilemma" and "people's dilemma" to explain the relationship between God's will and people's attitudes. When explaining this framework, state the relationship meant: God gives guidance, while people may ignore it, reject it or fail to carry it out.

In a simple explanation, we can ask: what guidance is stated? How do people respond to that guidance? What tangle comes from that response? This explains the author's term in the context of the discussion, without turning the term into an extra claim about God's nature.

Volume 9 lists seven spheres of problems: God with God; God with Iblis and the satans; God with people; people with God; God with the universe; people with the universe; and people with people. This list is a classification within the author's framework. It is different from the seven levels of presentation explained later.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 25–27 [PDF 114–116].

sections.heading: How to recognise the sign of a dilemma
paras: According to the author, the sign of a dilemma can be at the start of the ayat, at its end or in the meaning of the whole ayat. The reader must examine the words in their context. A single word on its own is not enough to set out the whole problem.

For example, the phrase "Afalaa yatadabbaruun" in Muhammad 47:24 directs attention to the problem of refusing to reflect deeply on the Al Quran. In Al Baqarah 2:186, the author draws attention to "la'allahum yarshuduun", then explains the problem of people's understanding and direction in life in their relationship with God.

A useful step is to read the whole ayat, identify the focus words, explain the problem the context supports and check the explanation against related ayat. Avoid fixing a meaning only because one word seems to fit the story we want to build.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 20–25 and 30–35 [PDF 109–114 and 119–124].

sections.heading: Four basic steps and seven levels of presentation
paras: Chapter 4 explains four basic steps. First, read the ayat and identify the words of the dilemma. Second, identify the problem raised. Third, explain the implied chain of events that suggests the cause of the problem. Fourth, discuss the solution and the benefit that results.

In the exam syllabus, this process is developed into seven levels: why the ayat was revealed as important; the signs of the chain of events; God's dilemma with people; the effects of the chain of dilemma; the path of the innovator's philosophy of the solution; the nostalgia of renewal in the solution; and the summary.

Both orders can be used together. The four steps give the basic way of working, while the seven levels arrange the content of a presentation so the importance of the ayat, the problem, the effects, the solution and its result are explained in full. For exam practice, Volume 9 also asks for three supporting ayat. How they connect must be explained, not just listed.
refs: Reference: Volume 9, book p. 28–29 [PDF 117–118] and 399–402 [PDF 488–491].

sections.heading: First example: Al Baqarah ayat 186
paras: Al Baqarah 2:186 states Allah's closeness, His answering the prayer of those who pray, and the call for people to respond to Him and believe in Him. The author uses this ayat as an early example of the method of Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul.

In the frame of that example, the dilemma is people who do not understand their relationship with God: not aware of His closeness, not knowing the role of prayer or not strengthening their faith. The implied chain can be explained as the state of people who face a need but do not know how to respond to the guidance of the ayat.

The solution links directly to the content of the ayat: understanding Allah's closeness, praying, responding to His call and believing in Him. The nostalgia the author describes is the sweetness of people's understanding in their belief in God. The reader can explain the change from ignorance to awareness and a more directed conviction.

A lesson to carry into the explanation is that prayer must be read together with the call to respond to guidance and to believe. This explanation does not set when or how each request will be met; it explains the link between the elements the ayat states.
refs: Reference for the author's example: Volume 9, book p. 30–33 [PDF 119–122].

sections.heading: Second example: Muhammad ayat 24
paras: This ayat asks: "Do they not reflect deeply on the Al Quran, or are there locks on their hearts?" The question leads the reader to the problem of attitude toward guidance and the heart's readiness to examine it.

In the author's explanation, the implied chain is people who have the Al Quran but refuse to understand and explain its importance in life. That dilemma produces a heart closed to lessons. The problem presented involves readiness to read, examine, understand and accept guidance.

The philosophy of the solution is to carry out tadabbur: examine the content of the ayat, discuss its meaning, check its links with other ayat and take lessons for action. The nostalgia sought is the change from closed to open toward understanding, and from neglecting to caring about guidance.

If this example is used in a lecture, a question for listeners could be: what does this ayat ask us to examine? What attitude blocks that examining? What change can we make after understanding it? These questions link the explanation to the effort of improving oneself.
refs: Reference for the author's example: Volume 9, book p. 34–35 [PDF 123–124].

sections.heading: Short example: Al Asr ayat 1 to 3
paras: In the part on lessons about time, the author links Surah Al Asr with the use of time and the loss of life. This example helps us see how the concept of dilemma and solution can be explained through a whole chain of ayat.

The dilemma is people's loss. The chain that can be discussed is time passing along with neglected chances and actions that do not build life. The solution must return to what the third ayat states: faith, righteous deeds, urging one another to truth and urging one another to patience.

In this explanation, nostalgia means the benefit of a more directed life when those principles are practised. We can give examples of using time to fulfil responsibilities, mend relationships or do useful work. These examples apply the explanation, while the basis of the principle must stay with the ayat.
refs: Reference for the author's lessons on time: Volume 9, book p. 4–6 [PDF 93–95].

sections.heading: Link with other methods
paras: The volumes of Al Fathun Nawa stress the concept of the Al Quran explaining the Al Quran. In this method, the links between ayat are used to clarify and check the explanation. The reader must show why a supporting ayat relates to the problem and solution being presented.

Ta'wiilul Ma'ani helps examine what the ayat wants to convey. Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul focuses on the problem to be shown and untangled. Khitab Hilalul Wasil helps explain the links between ayat and words. Syariat Khafiah, in the author's framework, links the call with conviction and practice in life.

Volume 3 also tells apart the explanation of a story from the angles of the reason for revelation, the outward event, the hidden meaning and the use of its lessons. This shows that a story can be read to know what happened and to examine lessons that are relevant to life.
refs: Reference: Volume 3, book p. 3–4 [PDF 84–85]; Volume 5, book p. 378 [PDF 443]; Volume 6, book p. 768–769 [PDF 837–838]; Volume 9, book p. 19 and 28–29 [PDF 108 and 117–118].

sections.heading: Summary to close the explanation
paras: Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul invites us to understand the problem an ayat points to, examine the effects of people's attitudes and work toward a solution through guidance. The value of this understanding shows when the reader can explain the problem clearly and link the solution with practice.

When reading an ayat, ask: what is stated? What problem does it point to? How does that problem develop? What is the guidance for solving it? What good can become a conviction once the problem is untangled?

In this way, the chain of events explains the situation, the dilemma shows the problem, the philosophy directs the solution and nostalgia shows the benefit of the improvement. That is the flow of understanding at the core of the concept of Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul in the author's framework.

sections.heading: Further references on linking ayat
paras: Volume 4, Introduction p. xxxix [PDF 39]; Volume 7, Introduction p. xxxix–xl [PDF 39–40]; and Volume 8, Introduction p. xlv–xlvi [PDF 45–46] repeat the basis of explaining an ayat through one or more other ayat. These references complete the background of the approach, while the definition and specific steps of Al Ashlih Asbaabun Nuzul are explained in Volume 9.
